query: Consider the following context: High entropy alloys have excellent wear resistance, so they have great application prospects in the fields of wear resistance and surface protection. In that context, which material can be used for adhere to the surface of a Cu matrix, and why?

generation.hypothesis: Integrating a graded Ni-rich interfacial layer between a copper (Cu) matrix and a high-entropy alloy (HEA) coating will enhance metallurgical bonding and mitigate thermal expansion mismatch, resulting in improved adhesion and reduced wear under high-friction conditions compared to a direct HEA coating on Cu.
generation.material_initial_state: A Cu substrate that exhibits limited wear resistance and poor adhesion when conventional direct coatings are applied.
generation.intervention: Deposit a graded Ni-rich interfacial layer (via physical vapor deposition or a comparable method) onto the Cu substrate, and then deposit a HEA coating atop this interlayer.
generation.conditions: Testing under high friction wear conditions (e.g., pin-on-disk tests) at moderate to elevated temperatures that simulate practical operational environments.
generation.structural_mediator: The graded Ni-rich interlayer, which gradually transitions from the Cu substrate to the HEA coating, thereby reducing interfacial stresses associated with differences in thermal expansion and chemical compatibility.
generation.mechanism: The Ni-rich interlayer forms robust metallurgical bonds with both the Cu and the overlying HEA. Its graded composition serves to absorb differential thermal expansion and minimizes the development of interfacial stresses and brittle intermetallic compounds, thereby enhancing adhesion and wear resistance.
generation.predicted_outcome: Samples incorporating the graded Ni-rich interfacial layer are expected to exhibit significantly higher adhesion strength and lower wear rates than samples where the HEA is deposited directly onto the Cu substrate.
generation.baseline: Cu substrates with direct deposition of high-entropy alloy coatings or traditional wear-resistant coatings that do not include an engineered graded interfacial layer.
generation.boundary: The beneficial effects of the graded Ni-rich interlayer might be compromised if the operating temperatures exceed the interlayer's thermal stability limit or if excessive intermetallic compound formation occurs at the interface, potentially leading to brittle failures.
generation.uncertainty: Optimal composition gradients, deposition parameters, and long-term thermal stability of the Ni-rich interlayer require further experimental determination.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples on Cu substrates: one set with a graded Ni-rich interfacial layer followed by a HEA coating, and a control set with a directly deposited HEA coating. Subject both sample types to standardized pin-on-disk wear tests and thermal cycling procedures over a range of temperatures.
measurements: Adhesion strength quantified via scratch or pull-off tests
Wear rate determined through profilometry before and after testing
Assessment of interfacial integrity post thermal cycling (e.g., delamination or brittle phase formation)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If statistical evaluation reveals no significant improvement in adhesion or wear resistance in samples with the graded Ni-rich interlayer (p > 0.05) compared to the direct HEA coating, or if the interlayer leads to severe interfacial degradation (e.g., extensive delamination or formation of brittle intermetallic phases) under test conditions, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

Abstract This article presents the high temperature tensile and creep behaviors of a novel high entropy alloy (HEA). The microstructure of this HEA resembles that of advanced superalloys with a high entropy FCC matrix and L1 2 ordered precipitates, so it is also named as “high entropy superalloy (HESA)”. The tensile yield strengths of HESA surpass those of the reported HEAs from room temperature to elevated temperatures; furthermore, its creep resistance at 982 °C can be compared to those of some Ni-based superalloys. Analysis on experimental results indicate that HESA could be strengthened by the low stacking-fault energy of the matrix, high anti-phase boundary energy of the strengthening precipitate, and thermally stable microstructure. Positive misfit between FCC matrix and precipitate has yielded parallel raft microstructure during creep at 982 °C, and the creep curves of HESA were dominated by tertiary creep behavior. To the best of authors’ knowledge, this article is the first to present the elevated temperature tensile creep study on full scale specimens of a high entropy alloy, and the potential of HESA for high temperature structural application is discussed.

The concept of high entropy alloys (HEAs) has allowed the exploration of large composition space of alloys, and is currently one of the most intriguing research topics in the field of materials science [1] – [3] . Recent studies have shown attractive mechanical properties of HEAs at cryogenic temperature [4] and room temperature [5] with excellent combinations of high strength and toughness, indicating their potential as the structural materials. However, the strength of single phase type HEAs were reported to be insufficient at elevated temperatures [6] . Several HEAs, such as CoCrFeNiNb x [7] and CoCrFeNiMo x [8] demonstrated that a moderate increase in tensile strength can be achieved by various precipitates. Development of high-entropy alloy (HEA) films is a promising and cost-effective way to incorporate these materials of superior properties in harsh environments. In this work, a refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) film of equimolar CuMoTaWV was deposited on silicon and 304 stainless-steel substrates using DC-magnetron sputtering. A sputtering target was developed by partial sintering of an equimolar powder mixture of Cu, Mo, Ta, W, and V using spark plasma sintering. The target was used to sputter a nanocrystalline RHEA film with a thickness of ∼900 nm and an average grain size of 18 nm. X-ray diffraction of the film revealed a body-centered cubic solid solution with preferred orientation in the (110) directional plane. The nanocrystalline nature of the RHEA film resulted in a hardness of 19 ± 2.3 GPa and an elastic modulus of 259 ± 19.2 GPa. A high compressive strength of 10 ± 0.8 GPa was obtained in nanopillar compression due to solid solution hardening and grain boundary strengthening. The attractiveness of refractory high-entropy alloys (HEAs) as structural materials stems from their outstanding mechanical properties, thermal stability, wear resistance and corrosion performance in hostile environments [ [1] , [2] , [3] , [4] , [5] ]. Recently, refractory high-entropy alloys have received significant attention in relation to high-temperature application in aerospace, defense, and nuclear power generation industries [ [6] ]. In fact, they were designated to replace traditional Ni-based super-alloys in applications such as gas turbines, heat exchangers, aerospace propulsion components, rocket engine nozzle [ [7] ]. HEAs are multicomponent systems that are composed from a small number of principal elements. They are usually composed from at least five elements with individual atomic concentrations that range between 5% and 35%. HEAs can produce solid phase solutions, mainly due to their configurational entropy and ability to be adequately synthesized [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. decision.trend: Early studies in high‐entropy alloys have mainly optimized bulk wear resistance by tuning compositions, processing methods, and microstructural architectures. For example, powder metallurgical routes combined with spark plasma sintering (as in PMC7515071) have been used to achieve dense, hard microstructures that perform well under high‐temperature wear conditions. However, while these approaches demonstrate excellent intrinsic wear resistance, the challenge of forming a strong, metallurgical bond to dissimilar substrates (such as a Cu matrix) has not been directly addressed. Traditional wear‐resistant coatings (e.g., Ni–based alloys) were found wanting because of adhesion problems and mismatches in thermal or chemical properties. Thus, researchers have progressively moved from simply improving wear resistance toward more holistic strategies that also consider interfacial compatibility.
decision.unsolved: The key unresolved issue remains how to engineer a high‐entropy alloy coating that not only provides superior wear resistance but also adheres strongly to the Cu substrate. The mismatch in thermal expansion, potential chemical incompatibilities, and difficulties in establishing a metallurgical bond between Cu and high‐entropy alloys are still open challenges.
decision.lever: design and implement a graded interfacial layer (for example, incorporating a Ni-rich or otherwise Cu-compatible transition layer) between the Cu matrix and the high‐entropy alloy coating
decision.why: This step logically follows from the trend and identified gap: while high‐entropy alloys deliver excellent wear properties when optimized by composition and processing, the next challenge is to ensure a strong, reliable bond to a Cu substrate. A graded interlayer engineered by surface/interface methods can mitigate thermal expansion mismatches and promote metallurgical bonding, directly addressing the constraints highlighted in the research question.
